subject: physics
title: Mass-Spring and Pendulum Periods
welcome_lead: Calculate T = 2π √(m/k) and T = 2π √(L/g) for two textbook oscillators.
meta_desc: A-Level SHM adventure on period of mass-spring system and simple pendulum.
final_note: Both periods are amplitude-independent — provided the pendulum stays at small angles.

concepts.def: sin θ ≈ θ; needed for pendulum SHM.
Pivot to centre of mass distance.

walkthroughs.h2: T from F = ma and Hooke
walkthroughs.body_html: F = −kx and a = F/m so a = −(k/m)x = −ω² x with ω² = k/m. Hence T = 2π/ω = 2π √(m/k).
Restoring force ≈ −(mg/L) x for small angles. So ω² = g/L, T = 2π √(L/g). Independent of bob mass.
For a 1-second pendulum (T = 2 s), need L ≈ 1 m. Doubling spring constant cuts mass-spring period by √2.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
options: Mass changes with location but weight does not.
The horizontal velocity increases over time because the projectile is falling.
Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the gravitational force on that mass (N) and depends on g.
Mass and weight are the same thing, just expressed in different units.

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.
Mass changes with location but weight does not.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.
Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.

mcqs.q: For a projectile launched horizontally, what affects the horizontal component of velocity during flight (ignoring air resistance)?
options: Gravity slows down both the vertical and horizontal motion.
The horizontal velocity increases over time because the projectile is falling.
Mass changes with location but weight does not.
Nothing — horizontal velocity stays constant; only vertical velocity changes due to gravity.
